explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Pilate, the Roman governor, asks Jesus, "Are You the King of the Jews?" (Matthew 27:11). Jesus answers, "You have said so." Pilate walked in with a yes or no question and got a short answer he had to think about.

Not this one, friend. The question is about a king, not a priest. Pilate asks, "Are You the King of the Jews?" (Matthew 27:11). The chief priests are standing right there bringing accusations, but the title Pilate raises is King.
Close to home, but no. Pilate never says prophet in this scene. He asks, "Are You the King of the Jews?" (Matthew 27:11). It's a question about a king, and Jesus answers, "You have said so."

Not quite, friend. The text says the opposite. When the chief priests and elders accused Him, "He gave no answer" (Matthew 27:12). No arguing, no rebuttal, nothing. I'd have been defending my cookies in the first five seconds.

That's right. Jesus doesn't argue back. The text says that when He was accused by the chief priests and elders, "He gave no answer" (Matthew 27:12). Picture a whole room of accusations and one calm, quiet man in the middle of it. I can't even stay quiet when the oven timer beeps.

Yes, friend. Jesus gave no answer, "not even to a single charge, much to the governor's amazement" (Matthew 27:14). Pilate had just asked if He heard how many charges there were (Matthew 27:13). I think he expected some kind of defense, and he got silence instead.
Not this time, friend. The text doesn't say Pilate got angry. It says Jesus gave no answer to a single charge, "much to the governor's amazement" (Matthew 27:14). Amazed is the word the text uses.
He stays put, friend. Pilate doesn't walk away here. The text says Jesus gave no answer, "much to the governor's amazement" (Matthew 27:14). The trial keeps going from there.

That's the word. "Now it was the governor's custom at the feast to release to the crowd a prisoner of their choosing" (Matthew 27:15). The crowd gets to pick. That one custom is about to matter a whole lot.
No soldiers walking free here, friend. The custom was to release a prisoner, one the crowd chose (Matthew 27:15). A soldier isn't part of it.
Not a servant, friend. The text says the governor's custom at the feast was to release "a prisoner of their choosing" (Matthew 27:15). The crowd picks, and the one picked is a prisoner.
Right on, friend. "For he knew it was out of envy that they had handed Jesus over to him" (Matthew 27:18). Pilate saw what was behind it. The text gives us his read on the situation, and it was envy.

Not fear, friend. The text names the reason: "he knew it was out of envy that they had handed Jesus over to him" (Matthew 27:18). Pilate saw through the chief priests and elders, and envy is the word he had for it.
Not duty, friend. Matthew 27:18 says Pilate "knew it was out of envy that they had handed Jesus over to him." Envy is the reason the text gives, and Pilate knew it.

explanations.answer: Have nothing to do with that innocent man
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Pilate's wife sends this message: "Have nothing to do with that innocent man…" (Matthew 27:19). She calls Jesus innocent, and she says it while Pilate is sitting right there on the judgment seat. The message comes from outside the room and says something loud and clear.

explanations.answer: Let the chief priests decide what to do
explanations.explanation: Not what she said, friend. Her message was, "Have nothing to do with that innocent man…" (Matthew 27:19). She says nothing about letting the chief priests decide. She calls Jesus innocent.

explanations.answer: Send that man back home to Galilee
explanations.explanation: No Galilee in her message, friend. She says, "Have nothing to do with that innocent man…" (Matthew 27:19). She calls Jesus innocent, and that's the heart of what she sends.

That's right, friend. She writes, "…for I have suffered terribly in a dream today because of Him" (Matthew 27:19). The text doesn't tell us what the dream was. I think it shook her up. I'd be sending that message too.

It's true, friend. Pilate's wife says, "…I have suffered terribly in a dream today because of Him" (Matthew 27:19). The text doesn't say what happened in the dream, only that she suffered terribly because of Jesus.

explanations.answer: Barabbas freed and Jesus put to death
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. "…the chief priests and elders persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to have Jesus put to death" (Matthew 27:20). They worked the crowds, and the crowds asked. Heavy stuff, and it's right there in the text.

explanations.answer: Jesus freed and Barabbas kept locked up
explanations.explanation: That's the flip of it, friend. The text says the chief priests and elders "persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to have Jesus put to death" (Matthew 27:20). It's Barabbas they wanted released, not Jesus.

explanations.answer: Jesus sent to Herod to be judged
explanations.explanation: No Herod in this passage, friend. The crowds were persuaded "to ask for Barabbas and to have Jesus put to death" (Matthew 27:20). That's what they asked Pilate for.
Yes, friend. When Pilate asks what to do with Jesus, "They all answered, 'Crucify Him!'" (Matthew 27:22). Two words, and they all said them. This is a heavy part of the story.

Not release, friend. Pilate asks what to do with Jesus, and "They all answered, 'Crucify Him!'" (Matthew 27:22). They had already asked for Barabbas to be released, so the word here is a different one.
Not spare, friend. The answer was, "Crucify Him!" (Matthew 27:22). The text says they all answered that way. It's a hard thing to read.

Not quite, friend. The text says the opposite. Pilate asks, "Why? What evil has He done?" and the crowd "shouted all the louder, 'Crucify Him!'" (Matthew 27:23). Louder, not quieter. Pilate asked a fair question and got a bigger shout.

That's right. Pilate asks, "What evil has He done?" and the crowd "shouted all the louder, 'Crucify Him!'" (Matthew 27:23). They don't answer his question. They get louder. It's a heavy moment, and the text doesn't soften it.

That's the one, friend. Pilate "took water and washed his hands before the crowd" (Matthew 27:24). Then he says, "I am innocent of this man's blood." Washing up in front of everybody is a loud move, and I think he wanted the crowd to see it.
No robe tearing here, friend. The text says Pilate "took water and washed his hands before the crowd" (Matthew 27:24). It was water, not fabric.
Not this time, friend. The text says a riot was breaking out, and Pilate "took water and washed his hands before the crowd" (Matthew 27:24). No soldiers are mentioned in this scene.

Yes, friend. Pilate says, "I am innocent of this man's blood" (Matthew 27:24). He says it while washing his hands in front of the crowd. Those are his words, and they sit right next to the next blank.
That's right. Pilate tells the crowd, "You bear the responsibility" (Matthew 27:24). He says it right after washing his hands. He's handing the weight to them.
Flip that one around, friend. Pilate says he is "innocent of this man's blood" (Matthew 27:24). Guilty is the opposite of what he says.
Not punishment, friend. Pilate says, "You bear the responsibility" (Matthew 27:24). The word he uses is responsibility.
Not ashamed, friend. Pilate says, "I am innocent of this man's blood" (Matthew 27:24). The text doesn't have him say he's ashamed. He says innocent.

That's right, friend. "But he had Jesus flogged, and handed Him over to be crucified" (Matthew 27:26). Pilate releases Barabbas, and Jesus is flogged. It's a heavy verse, and I think it's worth slowing down on.
Not chains, friend. The text says Pilate "had Jesus flogged, and handed Him over to be crucified" (Matthew 27:26). Flogged is the word. It's a hard verse to read.
Not prison, friend. Matthew 27:26 says Pilate "had Jesus flogged, and handed Him over to be crucified." He was flogged and then handed over. This is a heavy part of the story.
